title: How to Reduce Pubic Swelling After Tummy Tuck?
meta_description: Swelling is a common side effect of a tummy tuck and keeps going down until about 3 months. What helps in the pubic area and when to call your surgeon.
excerpt: Swelling is a common side effect of a tummy tuck. What to know about the pubic area, mons and labia, how long swelling lasts, the steps that help and the signs that need a call.
quick_answer:
How do you reduce pubic swelling after a tummy tuck?

Wear your compression garment as directed, usually for 4 to 6 weeks, walk a little from the day of surgery and avoid lifting for 6 weeks (Cindy Wu, MD, on the ASPS website). Keep your follow-ups. Swelling keeps going down for about 3 months, she says. One-sided, hot or fast-growing swelling needs a call.

images.text_in_image:
Swelling after a tummy tuck
Week 1–2: Swelling is expected; wear your garment as directed. Bruising subsides in a couple of weeks.
Week 3–6: Swelling gradually subsides. The Aesthetic Society says it should subside within 5 weeks. The garment is worn for 4 to 6 weeks.
By about 3 months: Swelling keeps going down until about now. The final result can take up to 3 months to show.
Healing varies. Follow your surgeon’s plan.
Sources. Bruising, garment and 3 months of swelling: Cindy Wu, MD, on the ASPS website. 5 weeks: The Aesthetic Society. Final result: Cleveland Clinic.

sources.publisher: ASPS website, a post by Cindy Wu, MD
sources.title: Answers to common tummy tuck questions (2019)
quotes: After surgery, you will be placed in a compression garment, which will be worn for 4-6 weeks after surgery to help with reducing swelling.
You can walk the day of surgery.
However, running or lifting should be avoided for six weeks after the procedure.
The bruising will subside in a couple of weeks, and the swelling will continue to diminish until approximately three months post-procedure.
Adequate hydration and ambulation are also important to lower the risk of blood clots after surgery.

sources.title: Tummy Tuck Aftercare & Recovery
quotes: Common side effects associated with a tummy tuck include redness, bruising, and swelling.
Swelling should subside within five weeks.
Call your surgeon immediately if you notice an increase in swelling, pain, redness, drainage, or bleeding in the surgical area, or if you develop fever, dizziness, nausea, or vomiting.
Other red flags include shortness of breath, chest pains, and an unusual heartbeat.
You will also need to wear a wide elastic compression garment to reduce swelling and provide support to the skin as it tightens.
It is important to walk to discourage swelling and to prevent blood clots in the legs.
However, avoid strenuous exercise for four to six weeks, because it can trigger unnecessary fluid retention in the treated areas.
It is also important to know that the amount of time it takes for recovery varies greatly among individuals.

sources.title: Tummy Tuck Scar
quotes: The scar for a standard tummy tuck usually spans your abdomen, from hip bone to hip bone, just above your pubic area.

sources.title: Tummy Tuck (Abdominoplasty)
quotes: It could take up to up to three months to see the final result.
Achieving proper nutrition can help your body heal.

sources.title: Jackson-Pratt (JP) Drain
quotes: Contact your provider immediately if you notice signs of an infection, including:
A fever of 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius) or more.
Sometimes, after providers remove JP drains, fluid collects and swells at the surgical site (wound).
This fluid is called a seroma.

sources.title: Vulvar Concerns in Women With a History of Abdominoplasty: A Case Series (2016)
quotes: We describe 5 women with a history of abdominoplasty who were referred with symptoms of vulvar pain, dyspareunia, lower urinary tract symptoms, and/or lesion/mass.
Abdominoplasty can result in anatomic changes to the female pubic region after elevation of the mons pubis and consequent elevation of the clitoris with or without retraction of the clitoral hood.

Although causation cannot be confirmed from this series, a temporal association of vulvar/clitoral pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and anatomic alterations with or without lesions after abdominoplasty was present in each case.
The aim of the study was to present a series of women with a history of traditional abdominoplasty or circumferential abdominoplasty (belt lipectomy) with vulvar concerns and anatomic changes.
